title: Breast Cancer Surgery
fit_question: Tell me about a time you navigated ambiguity in the workplace. Tell me about a time you demonstrated initiative.
prompt: A large medical-device corporation developed a disposable device to assist surgeons in breast-conservation surgery, the partial removal of cancerous breast tissue. It wants a revenue-maximizing US pricing strategy. What should it charge?

clarifying_info.answer: There are 100,000 US breast-conservation surgeries annually; the device applies to every procedure and a new disposable device is required each time.
It is FDA-approved, has no R&D quality concern, and has a 100% success rate.
There are no competitors; it is the only product of its kind.

interviewer_notes: Candidate-led case. The candidate must size the market and use clinician willingness-to-pay data to maximize revenue. Costs are not provided, so distinguish revenue maximization from profit maximization.

suggested_framework.summary: Book framework covering market potential, provider and insurer adoption, product differentiation and regulation.

children.label: Innovation, efficacy, quality and useful life

stages.interviewer_asks: How would you set a revenue-maximizing price?
stages.expected_answer: Size eligible surgeries, determine units per procedure, map clinician adoption at each price, calculate price × adopted procedures, and consider provider relationships, insurance, differentiation and regulation.

stages.interviewer_asks: What is the annual market potential?
stages.expected_answer: 100,000 devices annually because all 100,000 procedures are eligible and each requires one disposable device.

stages.info_to_release: Adoption at $0/$300/$600/$1,000 is 90%/75%/50%/10%; annual market is 100,000 surgeries.
stages.expected_answer: Revenue is $0, $22.5M, $30M and $10M. Charge $600, yielding 50,000 adopted procedures and $30M maximum potential revenue.
good_answer_signals: Does not equate maximum adoption with maximum revenue
Notes costs are needed for profit-maximizing price

stages.expected_answer: Use existing physician sales relationships, target large hospital networks, and advertise through TV, social media and specialty websites. Protect entry barriers with patents and clinician exclusivity.

Price at $600 to maximize revenue at $30M and target 50% adoption through physicians and hospital networks. Next calculate costs to find the profit-maximizing price and pursue patent and exclusivity protection. Main risks are imitation and confusing revenue with profit optimization.

exhibits.title: Clinician Adoption by Potential Price Point
exhibits.description: Candidate-facing willingness-to-adopt curve at four tested prices.
exhibits.key_insight: The $600 midpoint produces more revenue than higher adoption at $300 or higher price at $1,000.

math.question: Which price maximizes annual revenue?
math.answer: $600 per device, generating $30 million annual revenue

synthesis: Charge $600 per disposable device. At 50% adoption across 100,000 annual surgeries, revenue is $30M, the maximum among tested prices. Use physician relationships and hospital networks to reach adoption, secure patents and exclusivity, and add cost analysis before claiming this is the profit-maximizing price.
